title: in case
subtitle: in case you have a puncture / just in case / in case of fire
summary: Use in case to explain why you do something now because something might happen later, and tell it apart from if.

lesson.heading: in case something happens
lesson.text: Your car should have a spare wheel **in case** you have a puncture. This means: because it is possible you will have a puncture. **In case something happens** = because it is possible it will happen.

examples.text: I'd better write down my password **in case** I forget it.
examples.note: = because it is possible I will forget it

examples.text: Shall I draw a map for you **in case** you have a problem finding our house?
examples.note: = because it is possible you will have problems finding it

examples.text: I'll remind them about the meeting **in case** they've forgotten.
examples.note: = because it is possible they have forgotten

lesson.heading: just in case, and no will
lesson.text: We use **just in case** for a smaller possibility. We do not use will after in case - use a present tense.

examples.text: I don't think it will rain, but I'll take an umbrella **just in case**.
I'll write down my password **in case I forget** it.

left.label: in case
left.text: We use in case to say why somebody does something. You do something now in case something happens later.
examples: We'll buy some more food **in case** Tom comes. (= Maybe Tom will come. We'll buy the food now, whether he comes or not. Then we'll already have it if he comes.)
I'll give you my phone number **in case** you need to contact me.
You should insure your bike **in case** it is stolen.

right.label: if
right.text: With if, what you do depends on what happens.
examples: We'll buy some more food **if** Tom comes. (= Maybe Tom will come. If he comes, we'll buy some more food. If he doesn't come, we won't buy any.)
You can call me on this number **if** you need to contact me.
You should inform the police **if** your bike is stolen.

lesson.heading: in case + past
lesson.text: You can use **in case + past** to say why somebody did something in the past.

examples.text: I gave him my phone number **in case he needed** to contact me.
examples.note: = because it was possible that he would need to contact me

examples.text: I drew a map for Sarah **in case she had** a problem finding our house.
We rang the doorbell again **in case they hadn't heard** it the first time.

lesson.heading: in case of
lesson.text: **In case of** ... = if there is ... . It is used especially on notices and in instructions.

examples.text: **In case of** fire, please leave the building as quickly as possible.
**In case of** emergency, call this number.

lesson.text: Ask yourself when the action happens. In case = I do it now, before anything happens (take an umbrella in case it rains). If = I do it only after the condition comes true (I'll open the umbrella if it rains).

exercises.prompt: I'd better write down my password ___ I forget it.
exercises.explanation: I write it down now because it is possible I will forget it later: in case.

exercises.prompt: Sophie is going for a long walk in the country. Match each piece of advice with the reason for it.

pairs.right: in case you need to call somebody.

exercises.statement: I'll write down my password in case I will forget it.
exercises.explanation: I'll write down my password in case I forget it. We do not use will after in case.

exercises.statement: In case of fire, please leave the building as quickly as possible.
exercises.explanation: Correct. In case of fire = if there is a fire. This form is used on notices and in instructions.

exercises.prompt: It's possible that Jane will need to contact you, so you give her your phone number. What do you say?
exercises.answer: I'll give you my phone number in case you need to contact me.
exercises.explanation: In case + present tense (you need) explains why you give the number now.

exercises.prompt: A friend of yours is going away for a long time. Maybe you won't see her again before she goes, so you decide to say goodbye now. You say: I'll say goodbye now ___.
answers: in case I don't see you again
in case I don't see you again before you go
in case I do not see you again
exercises.explanation: In case + present tense: in case I don't see you again.

exercises.prompt: You're shopping with a friend. She's just bought some jeans, but she didn't try them on. Maybe they won't fit her. You say: Keep the receipt ___.
answers: in case they don't fit you
in case they do not fit you
in case they do not fit
exercises.explanation: Keep the receipt now because it is possible the jeans won't fit: in case they don't fit you.

exercises.prompt: I thought that I might forget the name of the book, so I wrote it down. I wrote down the name of the book ___.
exercises.explanation: For a past action we use in case + past: in case I forgot it.

exercises.prompt: I sent an email to Lisa, but she didn't reply. So I sent another email, because maybe she didn't get the first one. I sent her another email ___.
exercises.hint: (in case / not get / the first one)
answers: in case she didn't get the first one
in case she hadn't got the first one
in case she did not get the first one
exercises.explanation: In case + past to say why I did something: in case she didn't get the first one.

exercises.prompt: Which word fits the gap: in case or if?

items.text: I made a copy of the document ___ something happens to the original.
This book belongs to Kate. Can you give it to her ___ you see her?
Write your name and phone number on your bag ___ you lose it.
Go to the lost property office ___ you lose your bag.
The burglar alarm will ring ___ somebody tries to break into the house.
You should lock your bike to something ___ somebody tries to steal it.

exercises.prompt: I hope you'll come to Australia sometime. ___ you come, you must visit us.
exercises.explanation: Visiting us depends on whether you come, so this is a condition: If you come.

exercises.prompt: I was advised to get insurance ___ I needed medical treatment while I was abroad.
exercises.explanation: You get insurance before anything happens, because it is possible you will need treatment: in case (+ past here, because the advice was in the past).
